clue.text: High Street bank?

parts.note: bank here is not a place for money but the slope given to a road surface, and a street that is high in the middle has exactly that curve

explanation.walkthrough: A High Street bank is a British town-centre branch such as Barclays or Lloyds. The question mark asks you to take 'bank' as a slope and 'High Street' as a road raised in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: the slight arch of a road surface, higher in the centre so that rain drains off, is a banking of the roadway.

clue.text: Monetary unit of the marketplace

definitions.meaning: a small Israeli coin, one hundredth of a shekel
the public square where trade and assemblies took place in an ancient Greek city

explanation.surface: The currency in which the market does its business.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: an Israeli coin worth a hundredth of a shekel, and the open trading square of an ancient Greek city.

clue.text: Docked at the end, like a runner at Camptown

definitions.meaning: to dock an animal is to cut its tail short
in Stephen Foster's song Camptown Races the singer bets his money on the bob-tail nag

explanation.surface: A ship ties up at the quay as a racer finishes at a small-town meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked' suggests a ship in harbour, but it means having the tail cut short. The runner is the horse in Stephen Foster's song Camptown Races: 'I'll bet my money on the bob-tail nag'.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse with its tail cropped short is described this way, and the nag in the Stephen Foster song is exactly such a horse.

clue.text: Highly exciting and ruddy popular!

parts.note: ruddy describes a red complexion
something hot is in fashion and much in demand

explanation.surface: Someone raves that a thing is thrilling and, with a mild British oath, very well liked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' reads as the mild British swear word, a polite stand-in for 'bloody'; here it is simply the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: thrilling news or a sizzling performance is described with this phrase.

clue.text: Cry of pain in open carriage

indicators.note: in places the cry within the word that follows it

parts.note: bare means uncovered, open to view
ouch is what one says when hurt

explanation.surface: Someone yelps in pain while riding in a roofless horse-drawn vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'open carriage' reads as one phrase, and this vehicle really is roofless apart from a folding hood, but 'open' belongs to the wordplay and 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle with a folding hood, fashionable in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Bandit, about noon, pays for drinks in this charity event

indicators.note: about tells us the outlaw goes round the letter for noon

parts.note: a brigand is a robber who lives by plunder
whoever buys something pays for it
ale is beer, loosely standing for drinks

explanation.surface: An outlaw stands a round at midday during a fundraiser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts N inside BRIGAND. This is a British fundraiser where people donate goods and then purchase what others have donated.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a British fundraiser at which people donate goods and purchase one another's, the proceeds going to a good cause.

clue.text: Handle to adjust speed of clock

definitions.meaning: to handle something is to control or manage it
a clockmaker alters the mechanism so that it neither gains nor loses time

explanation.surface: A lever on a timepiece that makes it run faster or slower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a noun, the knob on the clock, but it is a verb meaning to control.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one verb: to control or manage, and to set a timepiece so that it keeps correct time.

clue.text: Gloomy in a place for retirement abroad

parts.note: un is the French for a, the foreign language being signalled by abroad at the end
lit is the French word for bed, where one retires for the night

explanation.surface: A dreary spot overseas in which to spend one's pension years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retirement' suggests pensioners settling in Spain, but it means going to bed. 'abroad' asks for French: 'a bed' is 'un lit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a room with no lamps burning is dark and dismal.

clue.text: NHS orange-crush for dependants

indicators.note: crushing something breaks it up, so the letters before it are mashed into a new order

explanation.surface: The health service supplies fruit squash to patients' families.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crush' is the anagram signal. The NHS is Britain's National Health Service, and orange crush is a fizzy drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: people who attach themselves to someone and live off them are parasites relying on another.

clue.text: Hostile because of the calling at bridge

parts.note: for can mean because of, as in famous for his wit
the bidding is the auction of calls that opens each hand of bridge

explanation.surface: Tempers fray at the card table over what somebody bid.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a stern, unfriendly manner or a grim, threatening landscape is described this way.

clue.text: Bar trade

definitions.meaning: a bar is a stripe or narrow band
one's trade is one's occupation or business, as in what is your trade

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: a stripe or narrow band, and a person's occupation or field of business.

clue.text: To follow language of the Philippines, include a neuter

indicators.note: include tells us the language takes the neuter abbreviation inside it

parts.note: Tagalog is the main native language of the Philippines
N is the grammar abbreviation for neuter

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson: to keep up with Filipino speech, add a neuter gender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'include' puts N inside TAGALOG.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to accompany someone by trailing after them, often uninvited.

clue.text: Bedding in disorder

definitions.meaning: straw or similar material spread for animals to lie on
a scattered mess of rubbish or odds and ends

explanation.surface: Sheets and blankets left in a tangle.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one noun: straw laid down for animals to sleep on, and an untidy mess of scattered things.

clue.text: Murder victim. Lincoln, left behind

indicators.note: behind tells us the letter for left comes after the president's name

parts.note: Abe is the familiar name of President Abraham Lincoln

explanation.surface: A president is assassinated and abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln was himself murdered, so the definition seems to describe him; the victim wanted is the biblical brother killed by Cain. 'behind' places L after ABE.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: in Genesis he is the shepherd son of Adam, killed by his brother Cain.

clue.text: From Belfry's first to the eighteenth, that's where they blow up!

indicators.note: first, after the possessive, asks for the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: on a golf course the eighteenth is the final hole of a round

explanation.surface: Golfers lose their temper all the way round a famous course.
explanation.walkthrough: The Belfry is an English golf course that has hosted the Ryder Cup. 'first' takes the B of Belfry's.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a boring drilled in rock to take an explosive charge, so quarrymen detonate it there.

clue.text: Wallet in coat seen to fall out

indicators.note: things that fall out end up scattered, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone watches a billfold drop from a jacket pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to fall out' is the anagram signal, working on COAT and SEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a folding pocket holder for banknotes.

clue.text: Chap on foot

parts.note: chap here is not a man but a sore crack in the skin, and the phrase names one that appears on the toes in cold weather

explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: an itchy sore swelling on the toes caused by cold, a kind of cracked skin.

clue.text: Charlie is expert on grass

indicators.note: in a down clue on places the first piece above the second

parts.note: crack means expert, as in a crack shot
pot and grass are both slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie knows all about lawns.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Charlie' is British slang for a fool. 'on' stacks CRACK above POT in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both are slang for a foolish or eccentric person.

clue.text: Crustacean badly barnacled, having no energy

indicators.note: badly says the letters of the next word are in the wrong order
having no tells us the letter for energy is dropped

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A sluggish sea creature is heavily encrusted with shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having no' removes E from BARNACLED, leaving BARNACLD, which 'badly' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a ten-legged shellfish that lives mostly ashore and returns to the sea to breed.

clue.text: Hostelries admitting people to the bar

definitions.text: Hostelries admitting people to the bar

parts.words: Hostelries admitting people to the bar
parts.note: pubs let drinkers up to the counter, and the four London societies of the same name call barristers to the legal Bar

explanation.surface: Pubs letting customers up to the counter.
explanation.walkthrough: In England a barrister qualifies by being 'called to the Bar' by one of four London legal societies that share their name with pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: pubs serve drinkers at a counter, and the London legal societies of Court qualify barristers.

clue.text: Things for silks and synthetic fibres

definitions.text: Things for silks and synthetic fibres

parts.words: Things for silks and synthetic fibres
parts.note: silks are senior barristers, who receive instructions for a case, and the same word names underpants made of silk or nylon

explanation.surface: Items suited to fine and man-made fabrics.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'silk' is a senior barrister (a KC), named for the silk gown; barristers are given written instructions for a case. The same word means underpants, made of silk or nylon.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: a lawyer's case instructions and close-fitting underpants share this name.

clue.text: Lacking normal tension in muscles, try a shot in the arm

parts.note: a shot in the arm is a boost or pick-me-up, which is what a tonic is

explanation.surface: A doctor suggests an injection for a patient with slack limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'try' only invites the solver to consider the phrase that follows; the injection is figurative, a pick-me-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Medical synonym: describes tissue that is flabby and without its usual firmness.

clue.text: I complain about Elimelech's wife

indicators.note: about turns the two words before it round to read backwards

parts.note: to moan is to grumble or complain

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a biblical man's spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns I MOAN round. Elimelech is the husband in the Book of Ruth.
explanation.definitionFit: Biblical fact: in the Book of Ruth she is married to Elimelech and is Ruth's mother-in-law.

clue.text: Clumsy GI taking London police time?

parts.note: the Yard is Scotland Yard, headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police
bird is British slang for a prison sentence, as is time

explanation.surface: A bumbling American soldier wastes the Metropolitan force's working hours.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's police; 'bird' is British slang for a prison term, from rhyming slang 'bird-lime' for time.
explanation.definitionFit: American military slang for a raw or inept recruit, often put on menial duties.

clue.text: Measure one's length looking at this emperor

definitions.text: Measure one's length looking at this
definitions.meaning: a marked strip of wood or plastic is read to find how long something is
an emperor is a sovereign who governs an empire

explanation.surface: A courtier falls flat on his face before his sovereign.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'measure one's length' is an idiom for falling flat; here it is literal measuring.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a marked straight edge used for finding how long something is, and a sovereign who governs.

clue.text: Old-fashioned sort of party doubled

indicators.note: doubled says the short word for a party is written twice

parts.note: a do is British informal for a party or social event

explanation.surface: A dated kind of social gathering, now twice the size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubled' writes DO twice. A 'do' is British informal for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: someone hopelessly behind the times is called after this extinct bird.

clue.text: Mercury, for example, effective in surveying instrument

parts.note: Mercury is one of the planets, so it is an example of a planet
able means capable or effective, as in an able administrator

explanation.surface: Quicksilver proves useful inside a surveyor's device.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a drawing board on a tripod used by map-makers for plotting in the field.

clue.text: Scoff at last minute?

parts.note: to last is to continue to exist, to be
minute, said my-NEWT, means tiny or little

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a thing done at the eleventh hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last minute' reads as the eleventh hour, but the words split: 'last' is a verb and 'minute' the adjective meaning tiny. The question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to disparage something, making it seem unimportant.

clue.text: Divers bask out of water

parts.note: to sun oneself is to bask in the sunshine
something out of water is dry

explanation.surface: Scuba swimmers lie in the sunshine on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' looks like people who dive; it is the old adjective meaning various.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an archaic adjective meaning several or various.
